title: The journey out of Africa
blurb: Small groups had left Africa before, but their lines mostly died out. Then, between about 60,000 and 50,000 years ago, one population moved out through southwest Asia and kept going. Genetic studies show that everyone alive today whose ancestry lies outside Africa descends mainly from this one movement, by a group that probably numbered only in the thousands.

links.label: Recent African origin of modern humans

dateNote: Genetic and fossil evidence put the main dispersal between about 60,000 and 50,000 years ago.

title: The giant animals vanish
blurb: As modern humans spread across the world, many of its largest animals disappeared. One study counted 177 species of large mammals, of 10 kilograms or more, that died out between 132,000 and 1,000 years ago: 62 in South America and 43 in North America alone. It found the losses closely tied to where humans lived and spread, with at most a weak link to climate.
debate: Climate change and humans both have broad support as causes of the extinctions, and their relative importance is still argued over.
dateNote: The extinctions happened at different times on different continents. The study behind this stop covers 132,000 to 1,000 years ago.

title: The oldest pictures and music
blurb: On a cave ceiling in Sulawesi, Indonesia, someone painted three human-like figures around a wild pig. Mineral crusts that grew over the paint are at least 51,200 years old, which makes it the oldest known picture that tells a story. More than 35,000 years ago, people in what is now Germany were playing flutes carved from bird bone and mammoth ivory.
dateNote: The date is a minimum age: the painting is older than the crust that covers it.

title: Meeting the relatives
blurb: The newcomers were not alone. Neanderthals had lived across Europe and western Asia for hundreds of thousands of years, and Denisovans further east. The groups met and had children together: people with ancestry outside Africa still carry about 2% Neanderthal DNA, from mixing dated to roughly 50,000 to 45,000 years ago. By about 40,000 years ago the Neanderthals were gone.
dateNote: The mixing is dated from ancient genomes; the last Neanderthal sites date to about 40,000 years ago.

title: Crossing the sea to Australia
blurb: Even with seas far lower than today, no land bridge ever joined Asia to Australia and New Guinea, then a single continent called Sahul. People crossed from island to island over tens of kilometres of open water, which took boats or rafts and planning. Stone tools at Madjedbebe in northern Australia have been dated to 65,000 years ago; other researchers argue for about 50,000.
debate: Clarkson and colleagues date the oldest tools at Madjedbebe to about 65,000 years ago. O'Connell and colleagues argue the tools may have moved down through the sand and that no site in Sahul is securely older than about 50,000 years.

title: The ice age at its peak
blurb: Between about 26,500 and 19,000 years ago the ice sheets reached their greatest size. Ice covered Canada and northern Europe. So much water was locked up in it that the sea stood about 125 metres lower than today. Britain was joined to Europe, Siberia to Alaska, and New Guinea to Australia. People lived through it on every continent they had reached.

title: Wolves become dogs
blurb: Dogs were the first domestic animal. Comparing the DNA of ancient people and dogs suggests that wolves became dogs in Siberia by about 23,000 years ago, perhaps while people and wolves were cut off there by the cold of the last ice age. Dogs then travelled with the first people into the Americas. By 11,000 years ago at least five distinct dog lineages had formed.
debate: The Siberian origin and the date of about 23,000 years ago are inferred from how human and dog lineages split and moved. Where and when dogs were first domesticated is still argued over.

title: Into the Americas
blurb: The Americas were the last continents people reached. A camp at Monte Verde in Chile shows they were far to the south by about 14,500 years ago, probably after travelling down the Pacific coast. Fossil footprints at White Sands in New Mexico have been dated to between 23,000 and 21,000 years ago. If that holds, people arrived before the ice age peaked.
debate: Whether people were in North America before about 16,000 years ago turns mostly on the White Sands footprints and how reliable their dates are.

title: The first pots, made by foragers
blurb: Pottery was invented by hunter-gatherers, not farmers. At Xianrendong Cave in southern China, pieces of pots date to 20,000 to 19,000 years ago, near the coldest part of the last ice age and more than 10,000 years before farming. In Japan, pots made by Jōmon foragers between about 15,000 and 11,800 years ago still carry burnt residues from cooking freshwater and marine foods.

title: The ice age ends
blurb: Layers of snow counted year by year in Greenland's ice record the end of the last ice age. About 14,700 years ago the climate warmed into a milder phase. Then came a cold spell, the Younger Dryas. At its end, 11,700 years ago, the ice records an abrupt shift: the start of the Holocene, the warm epoch in which all of farming and written history would unfold.
dateNote: Ice-core dates count years before 2000 CE, so 11,700 years ago is about 9700 BCE.

title: Bread before farming: the Natufians
blurb: In the Levant, Natufian hunter-gatherers lived from about 14,600 to 11,700 years ago. At Shubayqa 1 in northeastern Jordan they built a half-sunken house with a floor of basalt flagstones. In its remains, archaeologists found charred crumbs of flat bread made from wild einkorn and club-rush tubers, 14,400 years old: bread was being made at least 4,000 years before farming began.
